chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Humran, who said:

Camels were scarce for one year in Mina to the extent that a single camel cost one hundred dinars. So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about that, and he said, 'Share in it.' I said, 'And how much?' He said, 'Whatever is light (fewer in number) is better.' I said, 'For how many is it sufficient?' He said, 'For seventy.'

He (peace be upon him) said: We said to him, 'May we be your ransom, the sacrificial animals became scarce upon us in Mecca. Is it sufficient for two that they share in one sheep?' He said, 'Yes, and for seventy.'

The discussion regarding these narrations, despite the difference in their wording and meanings, is from two aspects. One aspect is that there is nothing in them indicating that it is sufficient for seven, or five, or seventy, according to the difference in their wording regarding the obligatory or voluntary offering. And if there is no explicit statement of that in them, we interpret them to mean what is not obligatory, rather than what is obligatory and binding, because that is not permissible; one [animal] is not sufficient for more than one, according to what we mentioned earlier. And that which indicates this interpretation is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the maximum number of people who can share one sacrificial animal according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tahdhib highlights the flexibility of the Udhiyah (sacrifice) during the Hajj season, where scarcity drove prices up, prompting Imam al-Baqir (AS) to permit sharing among up to seventy individuals. Shia jurists distinguish this from the obligatory sacrifice, noting that while one animal suffices for one person in mandatory cases, the 'seventy' limit applies to voluntary offerings, reflecting a pragmatic approach to communal worship. The commentary emphasizes that the permissibility of sharing is rooted in alleviating financial burden without compromising the ritual's validity.
